preview: An insightful internship experience at Barclays secured through the Barclays India Hackathon 2019, detailing the remote work adaptation, system migration project, and key learnings.
content:
INTERNSHIP EXPERIENCE
Nidhee Kamble
Computer Science, Batch 2017-21

Ye article informal hai. Mujhe jo laga, maine likha. Mujhe kisi ki tarafdaari ya criticism nahin karna tha.
Jitne aspects meri internship se relevant the (sirf kaam ya company nahin), woh saare hain. It’s a
subjective article(?); not an objective one.

-

The moment I see internship experiences anywhere on the internet, I feel like, ‘Is this another
cliche’. Oh how the turntables. Or I hope not:

My recruitment to Barclays happened through the Barclays India Hackathon 2019, in which I was a
part of the team representing VJTI. Barclays is a trans-Atlantic, UK-based investment bank and
financial services company. That’s the formal introduction of Barclays on Wikipedia and I couldn’t
frame it better than that. Including the hackathon, there were four rounds:
Round One: Competitive coding; submissions done team-wise. Duration: 3 hours.
Round Two: Competitive coding, topic-wise; submissions done individually. Duration: 3 hours, for 4
consecutive days.
The teams that qualified as an aggregate result of both the rounds, were called for the grand finale,
which was the on-site hackathon in Pune. The third and fourth rounds - technical and HR rounds,
respectively - happened during the hackathon (development phase) for all finalists. Internship and
PPO selections for the coming year were announced at the end of the final presentations. The
hackathon and recruitment results were independent.

The internship was (to) tentatively (be) in Pune in the summer after my third year (May 2020) and I
was looking forward to living on my own (yes that includes cooking and cleaning, and yes I looked
forward to that), working in a new environment, getting accustomed to new surroundings, and
discovering new places, habits, and people. Most importantly, I had decided to hog eat at good
restaurants (I had done my research beforehand) - a new one every weekend. Explore places.
But because of an unforeseen and greatly unfortunate pandemic (here comes the cliche), that didn’t
happen.

What did happen due to this stupid virus though, was all us interns getting a chance to listen to and
interact with the people at higher posts at Barclays, the sessions for which were specifically
organised. Managing directors or presidents or heads of sectors, and the like. That is something
that I think was the second best result of the Work From Home change. The first best result was
that I didn’t have to wake up and wear formals to go to work and come back and change again.
Barclays call these sessions Leadership Interactions. When you listen to people talking about their
experiences, you do come across adages and philosophies that are oft-quoted and heard. What is
new is how they take it and how it translates as a result of their perspectives. I liked that. I enjoyed
that. What I appreciated the most about these sessions is the absolute absence of
‘oh-don’t-talk-to-me-I’m-superior-than-you’ demeanour - which I’ve (sadly) seen prevail in some
organisations - and the fact that all of them addressed not only professional domains but also
personal ones. It makes you relate to them more as a human with their own thoughts having a life
beyond work, and not just as a senior colleague.

The induction included financial markets training - which included the structure of the company and
the introduction to (and familiarisation with) fintech (financial technology) jargon - along with
icebreakers. (Icebreakers were a separate thing and there were more than one.) My job in this six
week internship was to develop the solution design for system migration. There were things that I
was aware of, but most of the relevant learning happened on the job.
I would say the experience of working in your internship greatly depends on the kind of mentors you
get. In mine, mentors decided which project(s) were to be allotted to whom. I am happy that I had a
good mentor, and I didn’t feel overburdened or lost at any point. When I did, he guided me about
how I could proceed and was open to newer approaches to the problem as long as they had a
relevant reason. He also asked me a few days after the internship began if I felt like this is
something that I’d like to work on, or if I want it changed. Daily goals kept my spirit up and I enjoyed
my work. After a hiatus, I finally felt like myself during my internship, immersing into something that I
want to do. This project and my experience while working on it is what I remember when I look at
some of the subjects that I have in my Fourth Year. True experiential learning. When I read about
certain domains of them that I have already worked on, I feel free - no, not in the sense of not
having to study, but free because that knowledge has been empirical. I can grasp those things
better now, so studying them feels better than before. My experience has been helpful.

I was glad to discover during my internship, new aspects to the relations that I have, and what a
great difference they made to me in their own ways. My parents shared their inputs for my schedule
with me. My friends motivated me. My partner supported me. The people that I knew because of
CoC - my seniors and my (ex-)co-CoC-GS - suggested resources to me to help me learn the
required stuff better, and I realised the difference that having been a part of such a community in
college makes: you see things better. You approach them better. And you learn from and get
inspired by others who do or have already done it.
I also discovered - and felt proud of - my ability to adhere to work hours (as far as possible), and
give the time that I want: to work and personal life, both. This is something that I had decided to do
when my internship started and with passage of time, I began to learn things about managing it
better. Still am.

There are things that I learnt from colleagues, mentors, and the ones whom I heard share their
experiences; things that I learnt during my internship - both through my work and at the culmination
of it. It has been a month since my internship ended, and I still keep in mind and work on the
extensive feedback that my mentors gave at the end of six weeks.

I expected a pre-placement offer, but wasn’t offered one. I accept this decision. I learnt that things
won’t always go the way you expect them to, regardless of how justified you see your reasons to
be; and that there can also be things that your perspective perhaps limits you to see. I learnt that
accepting that is important. I am thankful to have had this experience too, and I am confident that it
will help me handle similar situations, at least a bit better.

Maybe I shouldn’t call internship experiences cliches. Writing about this has been insightful for me. I
am thankful for all of it, and glad about what I took from it. Like many other experiences that I have
had, this will be one that will stay with me. Ye sentence bhi cliche hi hai.
